variants.note: Common in neo-eclectic's applied brick and stone fronts; not a bearing material anywhere in the family.
No member of this family is a load-bearing masonry building; the whole family is production-frame construction from minimal-traditional's 8 ft precut stud onward.

construction_type.rule: The family is wood-frame throughout -- platform framing from the postwar period onward -- with masonry appearing only as a non-bearing veneer, never as a bearing wall.
construction_type.note: No member states 'construction_type' by name, but the technology is named repeatedly and consistently: minimal-traditional's own governing_logic names 'the 16-inch stud bay, the 8-foot precut stud'; ranch-style names 'the engineered light wood truss' and 'the 4-by-8 sheet of plywood and gypsum board'; neo-eclectic names the same truss and sheet-goods modules plus 'thin brick and stone veneer on a wire-lath backing' as its own applied finish. Marked judgment because it is inferred from consistently named technology rather than a slot any member addresses directly by this name.

window_grouping_rule.rule: All window heads on a given storey and elevation align to a single datum; where a genuine break in the wall or roof plane does not intervene, misalignment is this family's clearest and most repeated tell of a badly resolved elevation.
window_grouping_rule.note: neo-eclectic states this as an explicit zero-tolerance hard constraint (c03: 'all window heads on a given storey of a given elevation shall align to one datum,' with departures permitted only at a genuine plane change of 24 in or more) and names its own violation as 'head-height failure' in its long description. ranch-style's own governing_logic names the head datum as one of the only three things 'someone controlled by eye' to make a ranch read as well-proportioned rather than residual. minimal-traditional's own bound proportion pack note states 'the single-head-datum rule... still organizes what compositional discipline the elevation has' even in a plan-driven, otherwise ungoverned facade.

leaf_to_sash_ratio_min.source: minimal-traditional.c03 and neo-eclectic.c02, identical figure in both

shutter.rule: Where shutters are used, each leaf must be sized to plausibly close over the sash it flanks -- not less than 45 percent of the window's width -- hinged at the jamb, and omitted entirely from ganged, arched, bay, or non-rectangular windows. Half-width, screwed-flat shutters are this family's single most common and most explicitly named failure.
shutter.note: minimal-traditional's own hard constraint (c03) and neo-eclectic's own hard constraint (c02) state this rule in nearly identical language with the identical 45 percent figure. ranch-style does not restate the constraint directly but names the same failure as a diagnostic tell of its own later, degraded phase ('decorative shutters, scalloped bargeboard... applied to an otherwise unornamented long low box -- the 1955-1970 traditionalizing overlay'), so all three members converge on the same rule, two by explicit constraint and one by naming its violation.

variants.note: minimal-traditional's own strategy -- 'a detached garage at the rear of the lot, reached by a driveway beside the house' -- explicitly named in its own distinguished_from entry against ranch-style as the trait that separates the two nodes. Historically superseded within the family but not wrong; it is the strategy every later member abandoned once postwar lots widened.

ranch-style's own hard constraints (c01: setback not less than 4 ft behind the primary facade plane, or side-/rear-/alley-loaded; c02: garage door width not more than 33 percent of the street-facing facade) and neo-eclectic's own hard constraint (c05) restate the identical two numbers almost verbatim: 4 ft setback, 33 percent width ceiling, three-car garages split or turned.

The 'snout house' -- a garage projecting forward of the front door plane -- is named explicitly as forbidden by ranch-style c01 ('a garage face forward of the front door is forbidden') and is listed as neo-eclectic's own named diagnostic failure ('a garage projecting forward of the front door plane (the snout house), with the entry recessed behind it').

attached_setback_min_ft.source: ranch-style.c01 and neo-eclectic.c05, identical figure in both

attached_door_width_max_pct.source: ranch-style.c02 and neo-eclectic.c05, identical figure in both

garage_strategy.rule: This family exists because of the garage problem -- its own description names the unsolved street-elevation garage as 'the single largest gap in the traditional kit of parts.' Minimal Traditional avoided the problem by keeping the garage detached at the rear; every member built after it inherited an attached garage and converged, independently stated in two members with identical numbers, on the same fix: set the door back at least 4 ft behind the front facade plane (or side-/rear-/alley-load it), and never let the garage doors exceed a third of the street-facing facade. A garage flush with or forward of the front door plane is this family's most named and most repeated failure mode.
garage_strategy.note: The 4 ft / 33 percent figures are not an editorial synthesis -- they are the same two numbers, stated as hard constraints, in both ranch-style (c01, c02) and neo-eclectic (c05). This is as close to a genuinely measured family-wide commonality as this corpus offers.

projection_in.note: neo-eclectic states this range directly ('trim profile projection 1/4 to 3/4 in'); minimal-traditional's own casing is 2 1/4 in wide with 'a projection under 3/4 in,' the same ceiling.

casing.rule: Applied trim stays shallow in actual projection throughout the family -- well under an inch -- even as the applied ornament's scale and busyness increased sharply from Minimal Traditional to Neo-Eclectic. Real classical-depth trim (3 to 6 in of projection) is the family's own repeatedly named point of comparison and the thing it does not deliver, not a trait it shares.
casing.note: Directly quantified in minimal-traditional (2 1/4 in casing, under 3/4 in projection) and neo-eclectic (1/4-3/4 in projection, explicitly contrasted against the 3-6 in of 'the sources quoted'). ranch-style's own text does not give a trim dimension at all, and its own bound proportion pack notes that 'many built ranches in fact ran no applied interior trim at all' -- consistent with, but not independent confirmation of, the shallow-projection rule. Marked judgment because Ranch's silence is being read as consistent with, not as a third independent data point for, the other two.
